mappings.note: Natalya's jibe about catching black beetles is spoken in the play; retrieval, LO-1.
Why he cannot come to the point has to be inferred from his nervousness; the play never states it, so LO-2.
Asks why the quarrels are funny - the mechanics of farce, which is a literary convention and covered by no LO in this frame.
Her cry to bring him back is spoken in the play; retrieval, LO-1.
What happens to him when excited is described in his own lines; retrieval, LO-1.
The three hundred roubles valuation is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
The aunt's grandmother is named in Lomov's account; retrieval, LO-1.
Duplicate of the land-gift item; a stated fact, LO-1.
The forty years of use is a stated figure; retrieval, LO-1.
Natalya's claim of three hundred years is quoted in the play; retrieval, LO-1.
The brick-making peasants are named in Lomov's account; retrieval, LO-1.
Sending the mowers to the meadows is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
Justifying the title 'with reference to the characters and plot' requires the answer to be built from the play - evidence, LO-3.
'To what end does the playwright employ Lomov's palpitations' is a question about a dramatic device and its function - a literary convention, C-E1.4, rather than character analysis.
'Do you agree? Why/why not' about what the dog quarrel really shows - an opinion the learner must argue, C-E1.2.
Distinguishing 'looking to marry' from 'looking to marry Natalya' and saying what it shows about Lomov is character inference, LO-2.
Chubukov's embrace and blessing are staged in the play; retrieval, LO-1.
How the Oxen Meadows quarrel begins is narrated in the dialogue; retrieval, LO-1.
His suspicion of a loan request is stated in his aside; retrieval, LO-1.
His reasons - her housekeeping, their families' long acquaintance, his age - are all set out in his speeches; retrieval, LO-1.
Chubukov's delighted reaction is staged and quoted; retrieval, LO-1.
Who Lomov is and why he calls are both stated; retrieval, LO-1.
The two quarrels and their outcome are all in the dialogue; retrieval, LO-1.
Lomov's title argument is stated in his own words; retrieval, LO-1.
States the pronoun shift from first to third person in reported speech. A grammatical convention, C-E1.3.
Rewrites a newspaper interview from direct into reported speech. Grammatical transformation, C-E1.3.
Lists ill-effects of anger and ways to control it - the learner's own reasoning, C-E1.2, with nothing drawn from the play.

Drafting Lomov's matrimonial advertisement, and saying what would make Chubukov pick it, is precisely about rank and property as grounds for marriage, argued from the play - LO-11 - and rests on reading both characters (LO-2).
Invent a further quarrel and write it as dialogue. Composition in the play's register, C-E1.2.
Describes the first fight and the trivial grounds for it, all present in the dialogue; retrieval, LO-1.
The issues are retrievable (LO-1), but 'what does their quarrel reveal about them' is a character judgement (LO-2).
The change the falling snow works on the speaker of 'Dust of Snow' is the persona's inner shift, LO-2, which is not restricted to prose.
The crow's association with ill omen is what makes the poem's reversal work - symbolism, a literary convention, C-E1.4.
The hemlock as a poisonous tree carries the poem's bleak associations; symbolism, C-E1.4.
Recall of the poem's wintry setting. Verse recall, C-E1.4, since LO-1 is worded for prose extracts.
Frost's nationality is knowledge about the poet rather than the poem's content, so C-E1.4.
What the snow makes the speaker realise - that the day was not wasted after all - is the poem's message, LO-2.
The number of stanzas is a question of poetic form, covered only by C-E1.4.
Meaning of 'rued' as used in the line. Vocabulary, C-E1.1.
Asks for the poem's message about nature's healing effect - the writer's message, LO-2.
